name: Reversed Zeckendorf game: second-player winning starting numbers beyond n = 129 (OEIS A389618) and the Batterman et al. infinite P-position conjecture
compute_profile: laptop-minutes to laptop-hours (game DAG for n has at most A003107(n) Fibonacci-partition vertices; topological retrograde DAG search avoids the O(|V|^2) list scans of the 2023 reference code)
statement: The Reversed Zeckendorf Game, introduced by Z. X. Batterman, A. Jambhale, S. J. Miller, A. L. Narayanan, K. Sharma, A. K. Yang, and C. Yao ('The Reversed Zeckendorf Game', arXiv:2309.12748v2, 2023; Fibonacci Quarterly 63:2, 2025, 215-239) and catalogued by N. J. A. Sloane in OEIS A389617, A389618, and A389619 (December 2025), reverses the classical Zeckendorf game of Baird-Smith, Epstein, Flint, and Miller (2018). Indexing the Fibonacci numbers by F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2, F_3 = 3, F_4 = 5, ..., the game for a positive integer n >= 2 starts at the unique Zeckendorf decomposition of n into non-consecutive Fibonacci parts. Two players alternate moves under normal play (last player able to move wins), choosing either: (i) Split: replace one F_{i+1} with F_i + F_{i-1} for i >= 2, or replace one F_2 with 2 F_1; or (ii) Combine: replace F_{i-2} + F_{i+1} with 2 F_i for i > 2, or replace F_1 + F_3 with 2 F_2. The game terminates when all pieces are in the first bin (n copies of F_1). Batterman et al. proved constructively that Player 1 wins whenever n = F_{i+1} + F_{i-2} (Theorem 1.1) and solved starting positions restricted to {1, 2, 3} (Theorem 1.6), while posing Conjecture 1.2: Player 2 has a winning strategy for infinitely many n (and Conjecture 1.3: the limiting fraction of Player 1 wins is 1/phi ~ 0.618). Because the reference Python implementation in Appendix B of arXiv:2309.12748v2 used linear list membership (`if current_state in calculated_states`) and repeated full-graph scans (`while not_done`), their computation took 2 hours at n = 129 and stopped there. Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2 publishes for all 2 <= n <= 129 the exact vertex counts, edge counts (A389617, offset n = 2, displayed on OEIS through its 64th term n = 65 with 68,351 edges and tabulated in Table A1 through n = 129 with 384,715 vertices and 2,945,040 edges), 49 second-player wins in 2 <= n <= 129 (A389618: 3, 5, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, ..., 128, 129), and 79 first-player wins in 2 <= n <= 127 (A389619, which also prepends n = 1 as an 80th entry by OEIS cataloguing convention). As of 2026-10-30, no outcomes, vertex counts, or edge counts are known for any n >= 130, and Conjecture 1.2 remains open.
success_criterion: CONFIRMED: either (A) a machine-checked proof in Lean 4 (with no sorry and standard axioms) of Batterman et al. Conjecture 1.2 establishing that for infinitely many starting integers n >= 2, the initial Zeckendorf decomposition of n is a P-position (second-player win) under the Split and Combine rules; OR (B) the exact 1st/2nd-player outcomes of the Reversed Zeckendorf game for every integer n contiguously in 130..250 (yielding one table of outcomes, vertex counts, and edge counts for n = 130..250 that extends OEIS A389618, A389619, and A389617 through n = 250), computed by two independently written solvers using distinct representations that both reproduce every vertex count, edge count, and win/loss outcome in Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2 for all 2 <= n <= 129 and agree on every n in 130..250.

partial_wins.statement: Determine the exact 1st/2nd-player outcomes (extending OEIS A389618 and A389619) and exact DAG vertex and edge counts (extending OEIS A389617 and Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2) for every integer n contiguously in 130..180, verified by two independent solvers that reproduce Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2 for all 2 <= n <= 129.

verification_method: For Branch A, run `lake build` in Lean 4 and verify `#print axioms` on the main theorem proving that the set of n >= 2 for which the Reversed Zeckendorf game is a second-player win is infinite. For Branch B or p1, run two independent solvers from scratch (e.g., a topological-bucket retrograde evaluator in Python/C++ and a packed bit-vector hash-table DAG solver in C/Rust) implementing the exact Split and Combine rules of Section 3 and Appendix B of arXiv:2309.12748v2. Verify that both solvers exactly reproduce all 49 published terms of A389618 (for 2 <= n <= 129), all 79 terms >= 2 of A389619 (for 2 <= n <= 127), and every vertex and edge count in Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2 for 2 <= n <= 129 (including n = 64: 10,936 vertices, 63,222 edges; n = 65: 11,744 vertices, 68,351 edges; n = 129: 384,715 vertices, 2,945,040 edges), and that they agree on every vertex count, edge count, and win/loss outcome for all claimed n >= 130. Package the contiguous table extension as a single table file <= 1 MB (kit/SUBMIT.md).
angles: Every reachable state for a given n is a partition of n into Fibonacci parts F_1, F_2, ..., F_k, so the entire game graph for n has at most A003107(n) vertices. Replacing the O(|V|^2) list lookup and iterative relaxation in Appendix B of arXiv:2309.12748v2 with a hash-set BFS + reverse topological pass dramatically accelerates exact evaluation.

Every Split move strictly increases the total piece count sum_{i>=1} h_i by +1, while every Combine move leaves sum_{i>=1} h_i unchanged and strictly increases the weighted index sum sum_{i>=1} i * h_i by +1 for i > 2 (since 2i - (i - 2 + i + 1) = +1) or increases h_2 by +2 for i = 2 (F_1 + F_3 -> 2 F_2). Thus bucket-sorting reachable states in descending lexicographic order of (sum_{i>=1} h_i, sum_{i>=1} i * h_i, h_2) yields an explicit topological order of the DAG without recursion.

For Conjecture 1.2, look for starting Zeckendorf decompositions where every legal first move by Player 1 allows Player 2 to force the game into an all-even bin configuration (Lemma 4.1 of Batterman et al., where Player 2 wins by copycat) or a known P-position in the {1,2,3}-restricted endgame (Theorem 1.6).
pitfalls: Index convention: F_1 = 1, F_2 = 2, F_3 = 3, F_4 = 5 (there is no F_0 = 0 or duplicate 1). The Combine rule for i = 2 is F_1 + F_3 -> 2 F_2, and the Split rule for i = 1 is F_2 -> 2 F_1.

In A389617, the offset is n = 2 (the 64th displayed term is n = 65 with 11,744 vertices and 68,351 edges, while n = 64 has 10,936 vertices and 63,222 edges), and Table A1 of arXiv:2309.12748v2 already published vertex and edge counts up to n = 129; treat 2 <= n <= 129 as the calibration baseline and n >= 130 as the open frontier.

Under the normal-play rules, n = 1 starts at a single F_1 with 0 legal moves (a terminal position); Table A1 of Batterman et al. begins at n = 2, whereas OEIS A389619 includes 1 at the start of its list by cataloguing convention.
